title: New features
items: The README shows the app and how it fits together.
Updated the ServiceNow SDK and other libraries to clear known security alerts.

title: Fixes
items: The open-source copy is API-key only, carries no private names, and runs its checks on GitHub's own Linux machines.

title: Docs and SDKs stay current by themselves
items: The ServiceNow docs on your machine now keep themselves current: every day Wayfinder fetches changed pages, downloads the newest release when ServiceNow publishes it and removes older ones, keeping the newest and the release you selected. Settings → Pip → ServiceNow docs shows the last check. The SDKs Wayfinder is built on (ServiceNow SDK, Claude Agent SDK, MCP SDK) are watched weekly and arrive as a bump PR, then a release.

title: Full permissions on developer instances
items: A Full permissions switch for personal developer instances: Pip carries on without asking, and every change still shows in the chat and the approval log. Permission changes update open chats without triggering premature update-set refreshes during sign-in or access checks.

On a Mac, and on Windows (WSL), the secrets file is now sealed with a key kept in the macOS Keychain or the Windows Credential Manager, so a copy of the file alone gives nothing away. Existing files are sealed on the next start; WAYFINDER_KEYCHAIN=off keeps them plain.

Settings → Routines asks Pip the same question on a schedule (every hour, day or week), each run in a fresh chat of its own: new log errors, failed jobs, what changed this week. Routines only read the instance and count toward the daily budget.
Scripts now run straight from Pip's approval card, like Scripts - Background, with the output back in the chat. Set up the script runner once per instance in Settings.
Add your own MCP tool servers in Settings and Pip can use them alongside Wayfinder's built-in tools. Their tools always ask before running.

A polish pass on every screen in the Wayfinder design system: conversation text at 16px with a shorter line, headings that outrank the body, error and amber text readable in both themes, one tracking for every mono label, readable rail labels, hover and focus as the system draws them, thin quiet scrollbars, every animation off under Reduce Motion, and a chat's × reachable on a phone.
Scripts in approval cards preserve indentation, format compact code, and scroll in both directions, including saved approvals.
Setting up the script runner no longer fails on instances where custom Global APIs live under the company code (for example /api/1234567/...).
Setting up the script runner now works when a chat has switched to another app, and cleans up after itself if a step fails.

Settings: the admin flag now comes from the instance itself (gs.hasRole) instead of a role list it may hide; last login says why it isn't known instead of "? days ago". Pip's skills are edited in place, placement rules are cards you reorder, and What Pip learned, the Fluent cheat sheet and Speed read as one line each with the details folded away (rules are maintained on the Memory page).
Pip, the routines' schedules and update set notes now follow your time zone (the browser's), not the machine's. Settings → Pip shows which.

title: Wayfinder's own instance tools
items: Wayfinder now talks to your instance with its own built-in tools instead of NowAIKit: faster answers, tool calls named as Wayfinder's own, and no extra licence to think about.

title: Approvals answer only their own chat
items: An Approve or Deny click now goes to the chat that showed the card, and the server refuses it from any other chat, so with several chats running at once one chat can never approve another chat's change.

With several chats open, each approval card now names that chat's own update set and app, which is where the change will land. Before, a card could name the update set another chat had just switched to.
Picking Global (or any app) on the placement card now puts the new update set, and the work, in that app. Before, a new set could land in whichever app the account had open.

Pip no longer sees passwords, tokens, cookies or API keys in what it reads from your instance: they're masked in tool results (headers, URLs, JSON and XML bodies) before Pip, the chat or the saved history get them. Tables that store credentials themselves can't be read raw.

Each answer now reserves its share of today's spending limit when it starts (half of what's free), so chats answering at the same time can no longer each spend the whole remainder and overshoot the limit together. A chat that finds the rest reserved by other running answers is told to try again when one finishes.
Release checks reliably save and dismiss the intended memory suggestions, and release publishing starts with a valid workflow.

title: Pip opens ServiceNow pages for you
items: Ask Pip to open a record, list or any page on your instance and it opens in a new browser tab, signed in as you, with a link left in the chat. Pip doesn't read the page, and only your connected instance's pages can be opened.

Mockups of workspaces are now drawn by Wayfinder's own screen kit: Pip describes the screen (navigation, list, record, fields, tabs, actions, states) and the kit draws it with consistent styling at a real device size, labelled as a mockup with what's simulated and assumed. A screen the kit can't draw says exactly why. Free-form HTML is still there for concepts.

Each answer now has a working-time limit (10 to 45 minutes depending on the mode; time waiting on your approval cards doesn't count). Past it, Pip stops with a note and you can say continue. Pip's reviewer and researcher helpers have their own step limits.

Two chats working on the same app can no longer write files, build, save or restore checkpoints, or install at the same time; the second is told the app is busy and which step is running, and can still read the app. Edits during a running install wait until it finishes, so an install always ships the build that was approved.

Record change cards now show the update set and application the change will land in, read live from the chat's own instance, so a switch made in another chat on the same account is visible before you approve. Pip's instructions also read the current update set fresh at the start of each answer instead of from a ten-minute cache.
The approval log now also lists what the safety rules refused (not only what you clicked), each row tied to the action it belongs to, and passwords, tokens and keys are masked in it.

Weekly update set backups are written whole (a crash can't leave half a file) and now say when they hit their limits (200 sets, or 5000 updates in one set) instead of looking complete. The runbook explains exactly what backups and build checkpoints can and can't restore.

Generated app code now runs with an allowlisted environment, CPU and file limits and a capped memory heap, and is stopped together with everything it started. On Linux the Wayfinder checkout is hidden from builds too. App file tools refuse symlinks and the app's git folder. Install approvals say what the install receives (a token or your saved password) and whether it runs unsandboxed, and the docs now spell out what macOS and Docker don't protect.

Each answer's cost now counts only that answer. Before, a continued chat reported its running total under every answer, so costs and today's spending looked higher than they were and the daily limit could stop you early.

Deleting a chat now also deletes the Claude Agent SDK's own copy of it on this machine, which could include what Pip read from your instance. A new page, docs/DATA.md, says plainly what goes to Anthropic, what stays local, how long each is kept and how to delete it.

When the instance won't let Wayfinder check a plugin or Store app, it now says it couldn't check, instead of reporting it as not installed or not found. Pip is told not to conclude a product is missing from a failed check.
Two install or remove requests for the same app arriving together (from two chats, or a retry) can no longer both start; the second is told to wait for the first.
Wayfinder no longer names a company: the sidebar, sign-in screen, About and Pip's introduction just say Wayfinder.
Approve plan is now enforced: Pip can't write, build or install an app until you click Approve plan on that exact plan, and a changed plan needs a new click. Apps you already had count as approved.

Two chats can now change the same instance at the same time without mixing up where the changes go. Each record or script change first puts back its own chat's update set and application (another chat may have switched them), and changes from different chats take turns for the few seconds each one takes. nowaikit can no longer switch the update set for every chat; placement does it per chat.

title: Mockups show at their real size
items: Previews now lay a mockup out at a real desktop (1440 × 900), tablet (820 × 1180) or phone (390 × 844) size and scale it to fit, so the narrow side panel no longer squeezes a desktop design into its phone layout. Choose Fit or 100%, see the real size and scale, and open any preview full screen. Previews also can't load anything from the network.

title: Sending during an update just works
items: Updates no longer break an answer you send while Wayfinder is updating: the new version is built in its own folder and switched in at once, a message sent during the few seconds of the restart waits and goes through on its own, and if Pip can't start it says so plainly with Continue.

Pip now knows how to write flows in Build mode: a custom Action with a script step, a Subflow with inputs and outputs, and a subflow that calls another. It no longer burns trial builds guessing the syntax, and when something can't be written that way it says what to do instead.

title: Come back to Pip mid-answer
items: Leaving a chat while Pip is working no longer hides the work: come back, reload the page or open it on another device, and the answer picks up live where it is, with its steps, the build timeline and the board, instead of "Still answering in the background".

title: Build steps live in the side panel
items: On a wide screen the Build steps no longer sit as a bar above the chat: the timeline opens on the right as soon as Pip proposes the plan, and while it's closed a small chip in the chat header ("Build · 2 of 5 ›") shows where the build is and opens it again. Phones keep the bar.

Updates no longer cut Pip off mid-answer: an automatic update waits (up to 30 minutes) for running answers to finish before it restarts Wayfinder. If an answer is still cut off by a restart, the chat now says so and offers Continue instead of going quiet.

title: Docs and plugin checks are enforced before building
items: Pip can't skip its homework before building: planning, building or installing an app is refused until that chat has checked the ServiceNow docs and looked for an existing plugin or Store app, and Pip is told exactly which check is missing.

title: ServiceNow docs on your machine
items: Cited docs with one command: `wayfinder docs setup` (or Settings → Pip → Download ServiceNow docs) downloads and indexes ServiceNow's official docs on your machine, so Pip's answers link their sources with no docs server to run.

title: The board comes to you while Pip investigates
items: In a Debug chat, the board now opens by itself when Pip pins its first clue (once per chat; close it and it stays closed). Each clue shows its status as a chip, its controls only appear when you open it, new clues grow in, ruled-out clues stay in place struck through (older ones fold away past five), and the header counts the clues. Also fixes the board's Remove link, which showed as red text on a red box.

title: Watch your app being built, step by step
items: Build chats now show a timeline in the work area on the right: plan, write, build, install and test, each with what it means, ending in how many tests passed. It opens by itself on Pip's first build step (once per chat; close it and it stays closed), and the progress strip above the chat opens it again. Phones keep just the strip.

title: Fresh chat, spending limit and update-set note fixes
items: Continuing in a fresh chat twice in quick succession opens one chat, not two. Small jobs that fail or time out still count toward the daily spending limit. Update-set notes skip each app's Default set by its Default flag, are plain text, and name the account that wrote them.

title: Costs under each answer, and a daily spending limit
items: Each answer now shows how many steps it took and its estimated cost. Set a daily spending limit in Settings → Pip: Pip warns at 80%, and new answers wait once the day's limit is used up. Answers take fewer steps before pausing (Build 80, Debug 40), and when one stops at its limit it says so; type "continue" to pick up.

Pip now reads a short index instead of everything: the newest live clues on the board (ruled-out ones drop out), the newest saved items, and your memories in full up to a word budget, with older ones shortened until Pip opens them. Answers in big projects start faster and cost less. When a chat gets long, a note under the answer suggests a fresh chat for new work.

When a chat gets long, its note now has a "Continue in a fresh chat" button (also in ⌘K). The new chat starts from a short summary of the old one, with its open clues and where the work lives, so answers are quick again. When Pip has to summarise a long chat itself, it says so, and it keeps the changes you turned down, the changes already made and the decisions you saved.

Edit the placement rules in Settings → Pip, or go back to the shipped ones with Reset. Each rule now links to the ServiceNow docs behind it. A placement choice now holds for one instance only, so moving a chat to another instance asks again. Choosing a new custom app keeps Pip from changing records until that app exists and is current. Clicking the card twice no longer switches the update set twice.

Explore, Mockup, Decide and Debug now only read your instance; Build is where changes happen (records, scripts, plugins, installs, update sets). When a change is the answer elsewhere, Pip describes it exactly and asks you to switch the chat to Build. Debug keeps the investigation board. Answers outside Build carry fewer tools, so they're a little faster and cheaper.

After the first answer, a chat gets a short real title instead of the start of your message. A fresh chat now starts from a proper summary of the old one (goal, findings, decisions, what's still open). Titles, summaries and naming-convention drafts run on Haiku, the cheapest model, and count toward your daily spending limit; you can switch them to Sonnet in Settings → Pip.

At the end of Build work that changed records or scripts, Pip offers to add a short note to the current update set: what changed, why, and the risk. You see the exact text on the approval card before anything is written, and it's added after whatever the description already says.
A placement rule's doc link is shown only if it's an https address; any other link is dropped, with a warning in Settings.

title: One Memory page for everything Pip follows
items: The Memory page now shows every rule Pip follows in one place: your memories, suggestions you kept, your instance's naming rules, and what Pip learned from builds and failed tool calls.
Rules are grouped by where they apply (every chat, a project, this instance, building apps, using tools), each with a badge saying where it came from.
Pause a rule to keep it but take it out of Pip's instructions, then Resume it later. Edit or Delete works the same way, with Delete asking first.
Suggestions wait in a queue, one at a time: Keep, Edit then Keep, or Not now.
A rule that may contradict another is labelled, so you can pick one.
The top of the page says how many rules Pip reads and how many words that is, with a warning when it gets long.
Every answer says "Guided by N rules" underneath; click it to see them.

title: Pip asks where work should live before changing anything
items: Before Pip's first change in a chat, a card shows where the work should live: the app you're in, the app that owns the table, a new custom app, or global. It gives the reason, any warning (a licence note for new tables, cross-scope access) and the other options.
Pick Use, Another app or New custom app. Pip switches to the update set there for you, and remembers the choice for the rest of the chat.
The card flags when the table belongs to a different app than the one you're in.
Record and script changes wait until you've picked.
In Decide mode, ask "where should this live?" for the recommendation without a card.
The rules are a skill you can replace in ~/.config/wayfinder/skills/placement/; add your own test cases and run them with npm run eval:placement.

title: Pip reads its know-how only when it needs it
items: Build answers start lighter: the Fluent cheat sheet is no longer sent with every message. Pip reads it once in a chat, when it starts writing app code. That roughly halves what each Build message costs before code is written.
How Pip works in each mode now lives in skills you can change: put a SKILL.md with the same name in ~/.config/wayfinder/skills/<name>/ to replace one, or a new name to add your own know-how.
Settings → Pip → Skills lists every skill, where it comes from, and flags a file of yours it can't use (it falls back to the shipped one).
Only Wayfinder's own skills load; nothing from your other Claude setups leaks in.

title: Insights for admins and developers
items: Insights now shows development work instead of ticket counts: tables and fields, scripts, ACLs and roles changed in the last day, week or month, and update sets in progress (who, how many changes, and records that are in two sets at once).
Filter it by person or update set.
Log findings show the errors that are new since yesterday, grouped by the script and table that throw them.
Changes say what they touch, for example "x_loan.u_status changed type; 4 scripts and 1 flow read it", and looser ACLs are flagged (a condition or script removed, a role dropped).
New Impact button on each change: it opens a chat that maps what the change touches, with read-only checks and a link to each record. Pip can do the same search when you ask "what uses this field?".
Starter suggestions now follow the same direction (review, impact, access checks, ready to promote?). The sample-app examples are gone.

title: Update set: shown, not picked
items: The update set in the header is now read-only: Pip chooses and switches update sets as it works (each switch asks you first), so it isn't changed in the app any more.
It shows the set and its application, and lights up briefly when Pip switches it (it stays still if your system reduces motion).
Click it to see the application, state and number of changes, when and why Pip last switched it (with a link to that chat), and Open in ServiceNow.
The browser tab shows Pip's face instead of the old SN square, and phones get a matching home-screen icon.

title: Set up my PDI for me
items: New first choice when you connect a PDI: Set up my PDI for me. Give it the admin login once and Wayfinder creates its own integration user and sign-in, so there's no client ID or secret to copy.
It shows what it will add before it changes anything, and only goes ahead when you press Set it up.
The admin password is used for that one setup and never saved. The setup is in the activity log.
Personal developer instances only. Running it again reuses what's there and gives the sign-in a new secret.

title: Safer installs and updates
items: install.sh only runs once it has fully downloaded, so a cut-off download never runs part of it.

wayfinder update now goes back to the previous version only for what the release itself broke (Wayfinder starts, shows its version, saves to the board), not because your instance is asleep or a speed record is slow.
The daily update uses your WAYFINDER_BIN_DIR, and the systemd units work with paths that have spaces.
Windows: install.ps1 -Version 1.21.0 installs a particular version.
The README says plainly what the checksum protects against (a broken download, not a compromised release).

title: Clearer panels, room to type
items: Teach Pip, the Features search, board clues, interview answers and Compare's "why" are now boxes that grow as you type. Enter adds a new line; ⌘ Enter (Ctrl Enter) sends, and the box says so.
Features: one line at the top says what the panel is for, and each result says in plain words what it does and why you'd turn it on.

Board: a line says what it is (clues you and Pip pin while chasing a problem, read in every chat of the project). An empty board shows an example and how to add a clue, and a legend explains Open, Testing, Confirmed and Ruled out.
Projects, the mockup preview and Teach Pip each say in one line what they are.

title: No more duplicate instances
items: Connecting an instance that's already in Settings now updates it with the new sign-in, instead of adding a second copy of it.

Instances you no longer use can be removed from Settings → Instances. Their stored sign-in is deleted. Their chats stay readable, labelled with the old address, unless you tick the box to delete them too. The instance in use can't be removed.
On start, Wayfinder tidies away unused duplicate copies of your instance left by an earlier connect.
A chat from an instance that's no longer in use says so at the top.

title: One-command install and the wayfinder command
items: Install Wayfinder with one command: Homebrew on macOS, a curl line on Linux, or a PowerShell line on Windows (it installs inside WSL). Each download is checked against its published checksum.
A new wayfinder command starts, stops and updates Wayfinder, prints your login token, opens it in the browser and shows its log.
wayfinder update installs the latest release and goes back to the previous version by itself if the new one fails its checks.
wayfinder doctor checks Node, your folders, disk space, Claude and your instance, and says how to fix each problem.
Your data and settings folders are now private to you: they're created that way, and tightened on start if they were open to others.

title: Easier first start
items: Wayfinder now says up front what it needs: an Anthropic API key.
A PDI that was asleep now shows as waking up, not as an error. It takes a few minutes, and Wayfinder checks again by itself.
First-run setup says when docs answers come from the public docs site.
Wayfinder's default folders are ~/wayfinder-data and ~/.config/wayfinder. WAYFINDER_* settings replace SNW_*, which still work.
On a Node version that's too old, Wayfinder stops with a message saying which version to install.

title: A clearer Settings screen
items: Settings is now four sections: Instances, Pip, Safety and Advanced. Each shows its current state in the list, so you can see what is set without opening anything.

Each instance is a card with how it's signed in and what the account can do. Connecting another instance opens a form only when you ask for it, and it flags an address that isn't https while you type.
Secrets can be shown while you type them. Rotating the token, removing a learned rule and turning conventions off now ask right next to the button.
Long lists can be filtered, and the approval log shows the latest 10 with Show all. On a phone, Settings opens as a list; tap a section to open it.

title: Automatic updates say what went wrong
items: When an automatic update fails, the log now names the step that failed (install, build, restart, ready or smoke test) and shows its error.
On WSL, if the update can't restart Wayfinder because the systemd user bus has gone missing, it leaves the running version alone and says exactly that, with the fix.
An update that fails sends one notification per commit, if you set a notify command (see the runbook).

title: Memories guide Pip, but can't give orders
items: Saved memories now reach Pip as quoted lessons. Pip still follows them for how to work and design, but a memory can't approve a change, ask for one, or override Pip's rules, even if text copied from a record slipped into one.

title: Quicker, tidier update set backups
items: The weekly copy of your in-progress update sets now fetches a few sets at a time, so it finishes about three times sooner and is lighter on your instance.
It runs once a week, as intended. Before, every restart of Wayfinder (including each automatic update) started another copy.
Only the newest 8 backups per instance are kept, so they no longer fill up the disk. Two update sets with the same name now each get their own file.

title: Lighter on memory, tougher on big requests
items: Mockups and other live views free their memory when you leave them, so a long session with many mockups no longer keeps growing.
Wayfinder refuses oversized requests while they're still arriving (voice clips over about four minutes, anything else over 4 MB), instead of loading them into memory first.
Checking your login on each request is about four times faster.

title: Approval cards only look up real tables
items: Before you click, an approval card looks up the record's name so you can see what will change. It now only does that for a plain table name, so a crafted name can't make Wayfinder read some other part of your instance before you've decided.

title: Switching update set also switches the app
items: Fixed: when Pip switched to an update set, your current application could stay on another app, so new records landed there. Switching an update set now always switches the current application to the set's app (Global for sets without one), then checks that it took. If it didn't, Pip tells you which app to pick before making changes.

title: Long chats stay smooth while Pip answers
items: In a long chat, the page no longer slows down while Pip is answering. Earlier messages stay as they are instead of being redrawn for every word, and new words appear in small batches. In a test chat with 80 messages, the browser's work during an answer dropped from about 9.5 seconds to about half a second, with no more freezes.

title: Safer automatic updates
items: Updates no longer run the install scripts that come with Wayfinder's packages. The machine running Wayfinder holds your instance passwords and keys, so a tampered package can't run code there just by being installed. Nothing Wayfinder uses needs those scripts.
The automatic checks on each change now use fixed, reviewed versions of their GitHub tools, so a changed tool can't slip in unnoticed.

title: Pictures and notes can't leak or take over
items: Pictures from the web in Pip's answers now show as a link you can click, instead of loading by themselves. A planted image address could otherwise send instance data to another site the moment the answer appeared.
Titles of saved items and board clues now reach Pip as quoted notes, clearly marked as data, so text copied from a record can't turn into an instruction Pip follows in every later answer.

title: Approve exactly what runs
items: An approval card now shows exactly what will run. Every field and option Pip sends is listed, under "Also sent" or "Sent but not used" if it isn't a field change.
What you approve is what runs: the details are fixed when the card appears, each card can be answered once, and if the instance's address changes before you click, the change doesn't run.

Turning on automated test runs (ATF) gets its own card: "Set sn_atf.runner.enabled from false to true". It always asks, even in auto mode. Before, it couldn't run at all, or could look like an app install.

title: Instance addresses are https only
items: Wayfinder only connects to instances over https, so your client secret, password or session is never sent unencrypted. An older entry saved with http:// stops signing in until you change its address.

Changing an instance's address now works like connecting a new one: you sign in again, and a production or vendor instance needs the same tick-box as when you first add one. Auto mode turns off for chats on it.

title: Insights fits your phone
items: On a phone, Insights and the update set and docs menus open as a sheet across the bottom of the screen, with a × to close. Long rows wrap onto more lines instead of being cut off.
On a computer, the Insights menu now lines up under its button instead of running past the right edge of the window.

title: Every instance change asks first
items: Fixed: with writes turned on, Pip could change records through the "natural language update" tool without showing an Approve card or adding an audit entry. It now asks, like every other change.
Pip only skips the card for tools checked to be read-only. A tool it doesn't recognise, including new ones from a future update, asks first.

Record summaries and case sentiment can run a Now Assist skill on your instance, so they ask first too. So does NowAIKit's docs search, which sends your search text to servicenow.com; Pip's own docs search is unchanged.

title: Finished jobs tidy themselves away
items: Finished job pills in the top bar show a small ring that empties over 15 seconds, then the pill fades out on its own. No more clicking × to clear them.
Hover over a pill to hold it; tap the ring to dismiss it straight away. Jobs still running stay until they finish.

title: Your app's name, your team's conventions
items: Pip asks what to call your app before planning it, with a suggested name you can accept or change.
New in Settings → Your conventions: Pip can learn how your team names update sets, scoped apps, scripts, tables, fields and properties from what's already on your instance.
It only reads your instance, and you tick which rules Pip follows. Turn off clears them.
Pip then names new update sets, apps and scripts your team's way.

title: A cleaner Wayfinder on your phone
items: Phones get a slim title bar: menu, what you're looking at, and a + to start something new.
The menu slides over a dimmed page and closes when you tap beside it; the update set picker lives there now.
Mode buttons, example ideas and suggestions sit in one row you can swipe, instead of wrapping down the screen.
Chats on a phone: the title moves to the top bar, project and mode are two small chips, and result cards are compact.
Nothing spills off the side any more: settings, memory, projects and setup rows wrap neatly, and typing no longer zooms the page on iPhone.

title: A calmer, cleaner chat box
items: The message box is one line, the same height as its round send button (an up arrow), and grows as you write.
Pip sits centred on top of the box and says what it's doing right now, like "Searching the docs…" or "Waiting on you".
Stop, voice and queued messages use the same round buttons; the box lights up softly while you type.
Line breaks in your messages now show as you wrote them.
Tidier on phones: the chat title gets its own line and the "keep this chat" bar is shorter.

title: Pip learns from its mistakes, and reads logs in one go
items: When a call fails and a changed call works, Pip writes down the rule and follows it from then on. See and remove them in Settings → What Pip learned.
New log tool: one step summarises the system log (totals, top sources, repeating messages grouped together, an hourly trend) instead of paging through it.
Pip knows which date functions instance queries accept (gs.hoursAgo, not gs.hoursAgoStart), so log checks stop failing.
Fixed: Wayfinder's own checks were filling your system log with "access denied" errors; installed Store apps are now read a way your instance allows, so the Features panel sees them again.

title: One box to start anything
items: The home screen is one box: type what you want and press Enter. Auto picks the mode from what you write, or choose Build, Learn, Mockup, Decide or Debug yourself.
Three example prompts under the box change with the mode and come from your instance; click one to edit it first.
If Auto thinks you want an app, Pip checks before starting a build: plan an app, or look at options first.
No more questions before you start: after Pip's first answer, the chat offers to keep it in a project.
Your last chat is one click away: Continue, under Pip's hello.

title: Right update set, a cheat sheet that checks itself
items: Match my instance in the docs picker now finds your release.
The update set picker groups sets by application, and shows when Pip switches. Pip now switches to (or creates) a named update set in the right scope before changing records, asking you first.
Pip's hello on the home screen is about what you did last, with a button to pick it back up.
Chats started from a home card or Insights are titled with your idea, not Pip's instructions.
The Fluent cheat sheet Pip builds from checks itself: every example is compiled on each change and weekly on the newest SDK, and again here after an SDK upgrade.
Pip learns from build errors the cheat sheet didn't predict: once a fix builds, it drafts a rule and checks it compiles. You approve it in Settings → Fluent cheat sheet before Pip uses it.

title: Builds that get it right first time
items: Pip now builds from a checked Fluent cheat sheet instead of reading long SDK pages, so apps take fewer steps and fewer failed builds.
Pip writes all of an app's files and builds in one step, and fixes every build error in one go: errors come back with the file, line and a suggested fix.
Before creating an app, Pip checks the app scope isn't already taken on your instance.

title: A faster, smoother build loop
items: Interviews are a quick form now: tap answers, add a note if you like, or jump straight to what's already built in. Pip only asks what it can't sensibly guess.
Before building, Pip checks what your instance can do (like whether automated tests can run) and offers to turn it on.
After an install, Pip checks the app, runs its tests and gives you links to review, then asks what to change.
Install and test results show as cards with numbers, pass/fail lines and links.
Approval cards for record changes show the table, the record, its sys_id and the exact fields; once decided they fold to one line.
Pip's steps show as one calm row with the current step, folded by default. Cards in the chat no longer flicker while an answer streams.
The header has an update set picker and a docs version picker. Home has Insights → with what Pip noticed plus quick log and health prompts.
Enter moves wizards on. Press → to accept the faint suggested text while typing.
Settings → Speed shows, per mode, how many turns and steps answers take and how many steps fail.

title: Screens checked automatically
items: Behind the scenes: before each release, an automatic run clicks through the main screens (guided start, memory clouds, the approval dial, Features and Guide me, the ⌘K bar, What's new) to catch anything that stops working.

title: Fewer memory suggestions about Wayfinder itself
items: Pip no longer suggests memories that name Wayfinder's internal tools; those are bugs to report, not lessons to keep.

Behind the scenes: an automatic test suite now checks the safety rules (web allowlist, approvals, auto mode, installs), the access profile, Show me forms, the Features search and the memory checks before each release.

title: First-run setup and one-command install
items: A first-run setup walks new installs through three steps: test Claude on this machine (or paste an Anthropic API key), connect an instance, and see which optional extras are on.
Install with Docker in one command (docker compose up). Data and secrets live in volumes; it binds to this machine only.
A Start a new chat link sits next to 'What are we doing today?' for when you just want to talk.
Project files for going public: CI (typecheck, build, tests, changelog check, secret scan), SECURITY.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and issue and PR templates.

title: Easier to start, smarter suggestions, and a boop
items: Every new chat opens with a start screen: what the mode does, how to begin in three steps, and starters built from your instance. Mockup adds one-tap screen types (form, list, workspace page, portal page, dashboard).
Suggestions now come from what's on your instance (your newest custom tables, installed products, update sets in progress, today's log errors, unassigned P1s, apps built here), not fixed examples.
The home screen shows what's happening on your instance; tap a line to start looking into it.
Clearer labels everywhere: the rail shows a name under each icon, the chat header says Project and Mode, the Features search says Search, and each mode has a placeholder that tells you what to type.
Boop Pip: click it and it scrunches its eyes, bounces, and blinks twice.

title: Ready to share
items: Wayfinder is licensed under Apache 2.0, with a README (what it's for, how to connect, credits, license), a runbook, and a NOTICE crediting NowAIKit and the rest of the stack.
Settings → Speed now measures the first sign of life (a word or a step), which is what you feel, instead of only the first word.

title: Live mockups and rich answers
items: Mockups render live right in the chat (with a Code tab, Taller, Expand into the work area and Save), instead of showing HTML code.
Pip can answer with structured content when it helps: live views, cards, key-number tiles, step timelines, callouts and side-by-side columns, plus tables and images.

Out-of-the-box first, everywhere: before designing a whole app, workspace or portal, Pip checks what ServiceNow already offers on your instance and leads with those options as cards. One tap picks the built-in option or carries on custom.

title: What's new opens cleanly everywhere
items: On a phone, tapping ⓘ in the open sidebar now closes the sidebar and opens What's new on top, instead of trapping it behind the sidebar.
What's new always shows both ways out: × stays at the top and Got it at the bottom while the notes scroll. Clicking outside or pressing Escape closes it too.

title: Sign-in options and an access profile
items: Three ways to connect an instance: an integration user (OAuth client credentials, the default for PDIs), Sign in as me (OAuth with PKCE: you log in on the instance and your SSO, Wayfinder acts as you with your roles, and only a refresh token is stored), or a username and password (opt-in, for instances where OAuth isn't possible).

Access profile: Wayfinder checks what the connected account can actually do (who it is, its roles if it may read them, which key tables it can read, whether it can install plugins) and shows it in Settings → Instance → Access.
Pip works within that profile: it doesn't query tables the account can't read, says which role is missing instead of trying, and remembers anything the instance refuses so it never retries it.
Buttons follow the profile too: plugin installs and app installs are switched off, with the reason, for accounts that can't do them.
Pip knows an empty result can mean rows hidden by access rules, not that nothing exists (straight from the ServiceNow REST docs).

title: Faster, and measured
items: Every answer is timed: how long until Pip's first word, and how long each step takes (shown on the step). Settings → Speed shows the typical and slow numbers and the slowest tools.
Live updates: install progress, board clues, memory clouds, app status and job notes arrive the moment they happen, instead of on a timer.
Short caches for Show me field labels (10 minutes) and recent feature searches (2 minutes, cleared when a plugin or app finishes installing).
A smoke test with speed budgets (npm run smoke) checks a running Wayfinder after each deploy.

title: A new look, and Pip comes alive
items: New layout: an icon rail on the left (chats, board, features, memory, command bar, settings), the conversation in the middle, and one work area on the right for previews, the board and features, so panels never stack.

Pip is alive: its eyes follow your pointer and read along as you type, it blinks and glances around, ponders on hard calls, talks while it answers and hops when it's done. Settings → Pip: Alive, Still or Off (Off removes the character; answers come from Wayfinder in a neutral tone).
Guided start: pick a goal (build an app, learn, sketch, decide, fix) and answer one or two steps. For apps, choose a project, then 'Interview me first' or 'Just start building'.
Build chats show a live checklist (Plan, Write, Build, Install, Test) that lights up as Pip works.
Suggestions are now pills above the message box, and they follow the conversation (Approve plan, Show me the app, Run the tests…).
Approvals are a dial by the message box: Ask, Auto for an app, or Auto for the project.

Memory clouds: suggestions float up from Pip. ✓ keeps one, × sends it to the Memory tab's Dismissed list. Suggestions are smarter: never about Wayfinder's own tools, never repeats, at most one per answer.
⌘K command bar: jump to any chat or project, start any mode, or check a feature on your PDI.
Name your instance in Settings; the top bar links straight to it.
Feature search understands long phrases (it searches each keyword and ranks the results).

title: Voice, compare, and hardening
items: Voice: tap the mic, talk, tap done. Speech is turned into text on your own server; audio never leaves it and is deleted straight after. A sentence that trails off ("…and") waits for the rest.
Queueing: type or talk while Pip is answering and your message waits its turn. Send now stops the answer and sends it straight away.
Compare: tick two saved mockups in a project to see them side by side, then keep one; the choice and your reason are saved as a decision. App history can show the code changes since any past build.
Changed on PDI: an app card warns when someone edited the app on the instance after it was installed, before a reinstall overwrites it.
Cancel an app install from its chip at the top. After you stop an answer, Pip says what finished and what's still running.
Production or vendor instances can be connected with an explicit opt-in. They stay labelled, auto mode is off for them, and Pip is more careful.
Security: rotate the app token from Settings (signs out every other browser), and web fetches can never reach private or tailnet addresses, even for allowlisted names.

title: Investigation board
items: Board (top right): pin clues while chasing a problem (errors, records, log lines, docs pages and guesses) and mark each one open, testing, ruled out or confirmed.
Pip pins evidence and guesses as it debugs, updates them as it tests, and reads the board in every chat of the project, so you never re-explain where you got to.
One board per project, or per chat when the chat has no project.
Pin to board on any Show me card saves that record, its key fields and the live link as evidence.

title: Show me, checkpoints and auto mode
items: Show me: Pip can draw a record, its form or a list from your PDI right in the chat. Each card says when it was taken and what it leaves out, with Expand (a ServiceNow-style preview) and Open live on PDI.

Checkpoints: every good build is kept, and Pip saves a named checkpoint before big changes. An app's Details now show its history with Restore, which rolls back the source only; build and install again to put that version on the PDI.

Auto mode: in a Build chat, choose Auto for an app (or the whole project) and its installs and test runs go through without asking for two hours. Removals, plugins and anything the code scan flags still ask, and every auto step shows as an auto-approved line.
Install approvals now say what changed since the installed build, and flag risky code (system property changes, bulk deletes, outbound calls, security tables) worth a look first.
SDK docs are cached while the app runs, so repeat builds are faster.

title: Wayfinder: features engine and memory
items: The app is now Wayfinder. Pip is still its face.

Features panel (top right): search your instance's plugins and Store apps. Each shows whether it's on, ready to turn on, in the Store, blocked, or not available on developer instances, plus what it needs first.
Turn a feature on from the panel, or press Guide me for step-by-step setup from Pip, including what a PDI can and can't do.
Pip checks for out-of-the-box features before planning a custom build, and recommends turning one on or extending it when it covers the need.

Memory: Pip suggests lessons worth keeping (e.g. use Vulnerability Response's multithreaded job processor instead of a plain scheduled job). Keep or dismiss each one in the chat; manage them on the Memory page. Core memories shape every chat.
Credits and an independence note are in this panel.

title: Meet Pip, and a new look
items: Pip is the face of the app: it shows when it's listening, thinking, building, waiting on you, done or stuck. Click it to see what it's doing, or turn on quiet presence to keep it still.
A new look from the Wayfinder design system: near-black, one periwinkle accent, Geist type.
App builds and installs run in a sandbox that can't see your PDI key, your login or the network (installs get a short-lived instance token only).
An install approval covers one exact build. The card names it, and any edit after you approve needs a new build and a new approval.
What's new: this panel. A dot on the ⓘ button means there's something you haven't seen.

title: Projects and Build mode
items: Projects group chats, saved items and apps under one goal, with a brief that every chat in the project reads.
Save mockups and scripts from code blocks, and whole answers as decisions or notes.
Build mode: describe an app, approve the plan card, and Pip writes, builds and installs a scoped app on your PDI, then runs its tests.
Changing a chat's mode no longer fails.

title: First release
items: Chat with the ServiceNow docs and your PDI, with approvals for every change and a web allowlist you control.
Plugin and Store app installs run in the background with a progress chip.
Mockup previews, review and research agents, and PDI reclaim reminders.
